titleStmt.title: A Bandwidth Allocation Scheme for Time Constrained Message Transmission on A Slotted Ring LAN

analytic.title: A Bandwidth Allocation Scheme for Time Constrained Message Transmission on A Slotted Ring LAN

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We study the problem of transmitting time constrained synchronous messages in a slotted ring based local area network, carrying synchronous and asyn- chronous trafic. A bandwidth allocation scheme for synchronous messages is developed on top of a media access control protocol that assigns preemptive priority to synchronous trafic over asynchronous trafic. We derive suficient conditions for schedulability of time critical synchronous messages and show that the scheme achieves high levels of schedulable utilization. A slot access protocol is proposed for synchronous streams that implements the allocation scheme with minimal additional overhead and loss of schedulable utilization. The protocol is disiributed in the sense that any node can locally determine if it can use a slot, without exchanging any explicit messages with other nodes.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many safety-critical real-time applications like process control, air-traffic control, factory automation etc., must operate under stringent timing-constraints to ensure correct system behavior. A failure to observe the timing constraints can result in intolerable system degradation and, in some cases, catastrophic consequences. Such systems, in which the failure to observe timing constraints results in a fatal error, are called hard real-time systems. The inherent characteristics of many systems require that multiple, autonomous computers, connected through a local area network (LAN), cooperate in a distributed fashion. In such an environment, the end-teend deadlines on computations executing on multiple computers require timeconstrained message transmission.

In many real-time systems the messages may be divided into two classes, synchronous and asynchronous. The synchronous messages are periodically generated and are subject to real-time constraints. The asynchronous messages arrive aperiodically and do not have any real-time requirements. In such an environment, the primary aim of the real-time communication subsystem is to guarantee timely delivery of synchronous messages. In addition, it is desirable to have low response times for the asynchronous messages.

In recent years significant advances have been made in the area of real-time communication scheduling [l, 2, 3, 8, 15, 17, 18,22, 231 In many casea, the approach taken is to emulate centralized scheduling and exploit well known results from uniprocessor scheduling. However, the scheduling of hard real-time messages in a local area network is inherently different due to its distributed nature. As a result, significant overheads may result in attempting to maintain accurate global information. TO make the solutions scalable tu large systems with high speed transmission media, it is critical that the real-time communication schemes operate with minimal global state information.

A survey of various real-time communication protocols can be found in [lo]. They have classified the protocols developed into three categories: global priority arbitration protocols, e.g., [18, 231, global reservation protocols, e.g., [2], and bounded access time schemes, In this paper, we consider the problem of guaranteeing timing constraints for synchronous traffic on a slotted ring network. The slotted ring network has been used in Cambridge Fast Ring [6], Cambridge Backbone Ring [4] etc., and has also been standardized by British Telecom (Orwell [20]). It is particularly suitable for high speed local area networks [21] as well as hard real-time communication in high speed networks [14]. The allocation scheme is developed on top of a preemptive media access control protocol propoised in [13], supporting multiple classes of traffic on a slotted ring network. The approach used is similar to bandwidth allocation schemes for bounded access protocols employing time division multiplexing, such as FDDI [16] and TDMA [19]. In TDMA each station is allocated a fixed number of slots in each allocation cycle. Any asynchronous traffic must be transmitted within the assigned slots only. As a result, the asynchronous traffic is elevated to the level of synchronous traffic. On the other hand, in FDDI, a station may transmit asynchronous messages if the token arrives before the expected time. However, the asynchronous traffic may increase the actual token rotation time beyond targeted token rotation time (TTRT), thereby affecting the schedulability of synchronous messages. In contrast, since the protocol we use assigns preemptive priority to synchronous traffic, the asynchronous traffic may use any bandwidth unused by the synchronous traffic without affecting the schedulability of synchronous messages. A detailed study of this protocol for voice-data integration can be found in [ll, 121.
Here, we concentrate on guaranteeing deadlines for synchronous messages.

We propose a bandwidth allocation scheme for realtime communication of synchronous messages. The scheme divides the time frame into allocation cycles, and attempts to satisfy the average requirements of each stream in every allocation cycle. The challenge of the problem lies in the fact that the bandwidth must be allocated in integral units (slots), while the average bandwidth requirement may be non-integral. The naive approach of satisfying the average requirement in every cycle (i.e., by allocating the ceiling of the bandwidth required) may result in significant overallocation. To counter this, we use an approach similar to [9] which was used for pre-run-time scheduling of e.g., [I, 31.

We propose a distributed protocol to implement the allocation scheme. The distributed protocol allows each stream to determine locally, its allocation within a particular cycle. That in turn, allows each station to independently determine, whether it can use a passing free slot. The scheme can be implemented with minimal additional overhead. We derive a simple schedulability condition for the proposed allocation scheme. It is shown that the schedulable utilization increases as the length of the allocation cycle increases and asymptotically approaches the maximum achievable utilization.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The preemptive protocol based on a slotted ring is described in section 2. The bandwidth allocation scheme for synchronous traffic and its properties are discussed and proved in section 4. We propose a slot access mechanism to implement the bandwidth allocation scheme in section 5 and then provide some concluding remarks in section 6. ability of a slot by a station. The Control bits are used to implement the bandwidth allocation scheme and will be explained later. The Source and Dest fields contain the addresses of the source and the destination of the packet, respectively. The Info field contains the data packet, and the Acb bit is used by asynchronous message streams to acknowledge the receipt of packets. div.head: A& 2 The MAC Protocol
div.p: Packets arrive from external sources to the stations. Each station has separate buffers to store different classes of traffic. For the rest of the discussion, we call them sync-station and async-station for synchronous and asynchronous traffic, respectively. A station gets slots at regular intervals and may use free slots to transfer packets to destination stations.

A slot is considered free by a sync-station if the class field is Async or Empty. The sync-station writes the packet into such a slot and sets the class field to Sync. In the process it may overwrite a packet sent by an async-station. It also fills up source and destination fields of the slot. When the slot comes back to the source after a full rotation it is emptied by resetting the class field to Empty. Since there are a constant number of slots, a station can identify the slot it used by counting the number of slots passed by. When a sync-station receives a slot destined to it, it reads the information.

For asynchronous traffic, a slot is considered free if class field is Empty. The station sets it to Async, writes data in it, fills out source and destination fields, and waits for the slot to return. A destination asyncstation reads a full slot (class filled is Async) and sets the Ack bit. Note that the same slot is used for acknowledging the receipt. Since synchronous traffic does not modify the Ack, the acknowledgement is never overwritten. When the slot returns, the source station resets the class field to Empty if it is not Sync, and checks if the slot has been successfully read by the destination station by examining the Ack bit. If the bit is not set', the packet is retransmitted using the same strategy. The Ack bit is also reset by this station. Restrictions on free slot usage may be imposed to ensure fairness.

In this protocol, synchronous traffic is independent of the asynchronous traffic load. The residual bandwidth left after satisfying the need of the synchronous traffic is used by asynchronous traffic2. However, unlike reservation based protocols, the asynchronous ' traffic can make full use of variations in synchronous traffic load. At high synchronous traffic load, the bandwidth available to asynchronous traffic is low; when synchronous traffic load decreases asynchronous traffic gets a larger share of the available bandwidth. Consequently, the response time of asynchronous traffic improves, without affecting the schedulability of synchronous traffic.

div.head: System and Traffic Model
div.p: We consider a system of multiple computers connected via a slotted ring local area network. The slotted ring network has M slots and a ring rotation time of R.
Without loss of generality, we assume R to be 1.

We consider two classes of messagessynchronous and asynchronous. Synchronous messages arrive periodically and must be transmitted before their deadline. Asynchronous (background) messages arrive aperiodically and are not subject to any real-time requirements.

We assume that there are N streams of synchronous messages, SI, S 2 , . . . , SN. Each stream can be characterized as follows: A synchronous message arrives at the beginning of its period and must be transmitted by the end of the period. The period of a stream Si is denoted as Pi. Messages are packetized -the size of a packet is equal to the length of the Info field in a slot. The maximum length of a message from stream Si is Ci, denoting the number of slots required to transmit the message. Note that Ci is an integer. All streams are assumed to be in-phase, i.e., their first message arrives at time 0, the start of the first allocation cycle. Asynchronous messages are aperiodic and they do not have any real-time requirements. We say that a given set of synchronous message streams is schedvlable if there exists a mechanism which guarantees the transmission of all synchronous messages within their deadlines. We assume that there is a virtual station for each message stream. In the rest 2Use of the residual bandwidth to support data tr&c in a voice-data integrated LAN is discussed in [ll].

div.head: Synchronous Bandwidth Allocation Scheme
div.p: In this section we develop a bandwidth allocation scheme for synchronous message streams. We consider a slot allocation scheme in which the time-line is divided into fixed length intervals. Each such interval denotes an allocation cycle. The allocation of bandwidth to different streams, within each allocation cycle, must be done in a manner that guarantees the transmission of each message before its deadline. Clearly, a judicious choice of the cycle length is critical to the schedulability of the message set. In this paper, we choose the GCD of the periods as the cycle time. When the cycle length is GCD of the periods, each stream encounters an integral number of cycles within its period.

Let T = GCD(P1, P 2 , . . . , PN). We can write T = ( L + b)R, where, L is an integer, and 0 5 b < 1. Hence, in a single allocation cycle, there are L + 6 ring rotations. For convenience, we term such an allocation cycle to be of length L , denoting the number of full ring rotations.

A message belonging to stream Si must be allocated Ci slots within Pi/T cycles to successfully meet its deadline. The average (per-cycle) requirement of a message stream Si is thus given by T(Ci/Pi). Notice that while the allocation must be done in integral units (i.e., slots), the average requirement of a stream in an allocation cycle may be non-integral.

We define Vi = Ci/Pi, to be the utilization of the stream Si. This can be interpreted as the fraction of bandwidth spent in satisfying the need of the stream Si. We also define aggregate utilization due to all streams as:

In each allocation cycle, there are L complete slot rotations for each slot in the ring. When a slot is used by a stream, it is released only after a full rotation (due to source removal). The bandwidth allocated to a stream is, therefore, in terms of fullslot rotations. Due to this, the partial ring rotation in a cycle is not usable Consider the usage of a single slot. A slot released by a station can be used by another station downstream. However, in this hand-over process, a partial slot rotation is unused. This restricts the amount of bandwidth available for actual transmission of packets. It is therefore desirable to minimize the number of "hand-overs". Suppose that in a single cycle, stream Si is allocated Ij slots. To minimize the hand-over costs, each stream uses its full quota of Ii slots before releasing it. The released slot may then be used by the next station downstream. After a full cycle, the slot has undergone I 1 + 1 2 + + IN + 1 full rotations, the extra one coming about due to the summation of hand-over costs. This phenomenon is depicted in Fig- ure 2. The hand-over costs are shown as d i j . Note that the summation of the hand-over costs equals a full slot rotation. Thus, in one allocation cycle only L -1 slot rotations are useful. This is analogous to the token walk-time in token ring networks.

The above phenomenon can be generalized for an M-slot system. Each stream Si keeps a counter which indicates the number of slots it is allowed to use in an allocation cycle. Unless the counter is 0, a stream always grabs a passing free slot. Whenever a stream uses a slot to transmit a packet it decrements the counter by 1. Note that, the manner in which slots are accessed in a cycle depends on the configuration of the ring at the beginning of a cycle. However, irrespective of the configuration, each slot can carry L -1 packets.
Thus the aggregate bandwidth per cycle in an M-slot system is M ( L -1).

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: We presented a bandwidth allocation scheme for a slotted ring network for time critical messages. The allocation scheme guarantees timely delivery of synchronous messages. A schedulability test for the proposed allocation scheme was derived. We also proposed a slot access protocol which implements the allocation scheme with minimal additional overhead and loss of schedulable utilization. The protocol is distributed in the sense that any node can locally determine if it can use a slot, without exchanging any explicit message with other nodes. It is shown that a set of synchronous messages can be scheduled as long as the total utilization does not exceed an upper bound. The upper bound increases as the length of the allocation cycle increases and asymptotically reaches the maximum achievable utilization. The proposed allocation scheme uses the GCD of the periods of synchronous message streams as the cycle length. In many real-time systems, the periods are harmonic and would yield a large GCD. Even when the periods are not harmonic, it is not unreasonable to expect a GCD of the order of a few milliseconds. Since the ring rotation times are typically of the order of a few microseconds, the proposed allocation scheme would yield very high level of schedulability for such systems. However, it is still conceivable that the GCD of the periods may be arbitrarily small for some systems. Such systems would require a scheme in which the cycle time is not the GCD.

The scheme, as presented, makes strong assumption about the nature of synchronous streams. However, the scheme can be easily extended to cater for (i) arbitrary cycle lengths, (ii) deadlines smaller than periods, and (iii) no assumptions about phases of the streams. This is done as follows: first compute the average requirement of a stream based on the minimum number of allocation cycles a message may encounter before its deadline. If the sum of the requirements is within the available bandwidth in a cycle then the message set is schedulable.
